**EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

ForeSeeMe is an AI-assisted mobile health application designed to bridge the critical gap between regional disease surveillance and individual medication adherence in developing nations. Current public health systems in the region operate reactively, announcing outbreaks only after infection rates have peaked, while existing medication apps function as static alarms with no environmental awareness. ForeSeeMe addresses both challenges in a single unified platform by leveraging supervised machine learning models trained on historical disease incidence and environmental data (temperature, humidity, rainfall, air quality) to classify regional disease risk levels as Low, Medium, or High for selected cities. The Flutter-based mobile application enables users to create health profiles, manage medication schedules, and receive context-aware personalized alerts when environmental conditions indicate elevated risk in their area. A geospatial heatmap dashboard visualizes risk zones, and a Health Resource Center provides verified self-care guidelines and emergency contacts. The significance of this project lies in its ability to transform passive public health data into proactive, personalized preparedness reducing the burden of preventable diseases through timely behavioral interventions.

**Abstract**        

The primary rationale for developing ForeSeeMe is to bridge the critical disconnect between reactive public health surveillance and individual medication adherence in developing nations. Currently, disease surveillance systems in the region operate in silos, often announcing outbreaks only after infection rates have peaked. On the individual level, mobile health applications function primarily as static alarm clocks, tracking schedules without any awareness of environmental factors. Consequently, vulnerable populations remain unaware of rising regional risks until it is too late to take preventative measures. This lack of contextual awareness leads to poor medication adherence and increased susceptibility to preventable complications during high-risk periods. A significant gap exists in the lack of a unified platform that interprets macro-level disease trends to trigger micro-level personal health interventions. To address this, the proposed project aims to develop an AI-assisted system that analyzes historical health patterns and environmental conditions to estimate regional disease risk levels. It will simultaneously provide a user-friendly mobile interface for rigorous medication scheduling and tracking. Crucially, the system seeks to implement a context-aware alert mechanism that dynamically warns users to take extra precautions when environmental conditions indicate elevated regional health risk. The significance of this project lies in its ability to transform static health data into actionable, personalized preparedness, thereby reducing the burden of infectious diseases through proactive behavior modification.

# **Chapter 1: Introduction and Project Overview** {#chapter-1:-introduction-and-project-overview}

This chapter introduces ForeSeeMe as a system and sets the context for the requirements documented in Chapter 2\. It covers the background of the project, the problem being addressed, the proposed solution, project objectives, scope, modules, related systems, tools and technologies, and the project contribution.

## **1.1 Overview of the Project** {#1.1-overview-of-the-project}

ForeSeeMe is a Flutter-based mobile application designed to bridge two connected but currently separate problems in public health. On one side, disease surveillance in Pakistan operates reactively outbreaks like Dengue or smog-related respiratory illness only get announced after they have already spread. On the other side, patients with chronic conditions rely on basic alarm-clock apps to manage their medications, and those apps have zero awareness of what is happening in the surrounding environment.

The system addresses both gaps together. A supervised machine learning engine, built in Python using Scikit-learn, is trained on historical public health and environmental data to estimate relative disease risk levels for specific cities. These estimations classified as Low, Medium, or High are then used to trigger personalized push notifications to users who are in high-risk zones and have relevant health vulnerabilities on their profile.

This dual-track approach is what makes ForeSeeMe different from anything currently available. Existing solutions either focus on population-level surveillance for researchers and governments, or they handle individual medication reminders without any environmental context. ForeSeeMe connects those two layers into one platform for everyday users.

## **1.2 Vision Statement** {#1.2-vision-statement}

For individuals with chronic conditions and health-conscious citizens who struggle to maintain medication adherence and lack timely warnings about rising environmental health risks, ForeSeeMe is an AI-assisted disease risk awareness and medication management application that estimates regional disease risk levels and triggers personalized, context-aware alerts to ensure timely medication intake. Unlike fragmented solutions that offer either complex epidemiological dashboards for researchers or static, context-blind alarm clocks for patients, ForeSeeMe integrates predictive public health intelligence directly with personal adherence tracking, empowering users to take proactive, informed actions to protect their health before an outbreak peaks.

## **1.3 Problem Statement** {#1.3-problem-statement}

Despite advances in public health surveillance, disease risk detection in developing regions like Pakistan occurs too late for individuals to take meaningful preventive action. Outbreaks are typically identified only after infection rates have already peaked within a community, leading to increased morbidity that could have been reduced with earlier warnings.

At the individual level, patients with chronic conditions struggle to maintain strict medication adherence. This challenge compounds during outbreak periods when timely medication intake and specific health precautions become critical. Existing apps that try to help with this function as static alarm clocks. They have no awareness of the local environment and send the same reminder regardless of whether the air quality index is normal or dangerously high.

The core problem is that current solutions operate in silos. Public health surveillance systems give macro-level trend data to professionals, and medication apps give micro-level scheduling to individual users, but there is no unified platform that connects macro environmental signals to micro personal health behavior. Vulnerable users remain unaware of rising risks in their own city and fail to take extra precautions that could prevent complications. ForeSeeMe is built specifically to close that gap.

## **1.4 Problem Solution** {#1.4-problem-solution}

ForeSeeMe solves the problem through a three-part approach. First, a Python-based data pipeline aggregates historical health and environmental datasets, preprocesses them, and feeds them into a supervised machine learning model to classify regional disease risk levels. Second, a Flutter mobile application provides users with a clean interface to set up medication schedules, confirm daily doses, and track their adherence history. Third, a backend context logic engine cross-references each user's registered city and health vulnerabilities with the current ML-generated risk estimate and dispatches targeted push notifications via Firebase Cloud Messaging.

Instead of getting a generic reminder, a user registered as an Asthma patient in Lahore will receive a specific alert indicating that smog risk is high in their area and that they should take extra precautions. That is the core value the system delivers. The system also includes a Health Resource Center with verified precautionary content, a geospatial heatmap dashboard for visualizing risk zones, and integration with the Google Places API to surface nearby hospitals during high-risk alert periods.

## **1.5 Objectives of the Proposed System** {#1.5-objectives-of-the-proposed-system}

The primary objectives of ForeSeeMe are as follows:

1. PO-1: To estimate regional disease risk levels (Low, Medium, High) using supervised machine learning models trained on historical public health and environmental data such as temperature, humidity, rainfall, and air quality.

2. PO-2: To improve individual medication adherence through a dedicated scheduling and tracking mobile interface that logs daily doses and provides a personal adherence history.

3. PO-3: To deliver personalized, context-aware push notifications to vulnerable users when local environmental conditions indicate elevated regional health risk.

4. PO-4: To visualize active disease risk zones on an interactive geospatial dashboard using color-coded heatmaps to improve public awareness.

5. PO-5: To provide immediate access to verified self-care guidelines, precautionary tips, emergency contact numbers, and nearby healthcare facilities.

## **1.6 Scope** {#1.6-scope}

The scope of ForeSeeMe is to develop a user-centric, AI-assisted decision-support system that improves individual health preparedness by estimating regional disease risk levels and supporting medication adherence. The system does not perform epidemiological outbreak predictions or medical diagnosis. It classifies relative health risk levels for selected regions using supervised machine learning models trained on historical disease incidence and environmental data.

To ensure technical feasibility and clear environmental correlation, the system focuses on diseases whose occurrence is known to be influenced by environmental conditions specifically dengue fever, influenza-like illness, and smog-related respiratory risks. The platform is implemented as a Flutter-based mobile application. A FastAPI microservice in Python serves the trained ML model through REST endpoints. Firebase handles authentication, the Firestore database, and push notifications. Google Maps SDK renders the risk heatmap, and Google Places API surfaces nearby healthcare facilities during elevated alerts.

ForeSeeMe functions strictly as a health awareness and preparedness tool. It does not interpret individual symptoms, provide clinical recommendations, or replace official public health surveillance systems.

### **1.6.1 Limitations and Constraints** {#1.6.1-limitations-and-constraints}

**LI-1:** ForeSeeMe functions solely as a health awareness and decision-support tool. It does not interpret symptoms, provide medical diagnoses, or replace professional healthcare advice.

**LI-2:** Risk estimations depend on the availability and update frequency of public health and environmental datasets. Real-time weather API data is used, but official disease incidence data may have reporting delays.

**LI-3:** Initial deployment focuses on major metropolitan areas where reliable historical health and environmental data are available. Expanding to additional regions requires consistent datasets for accurate modelling.

**LI-4:** The AI engine uses classical supervised machine learning models such as Random Forest. Computationally intensive deep learning models are outside the scope of this implementation.

**LI-5:** Medication adherence is recorded based on user confirmation within the application. The system cannot physically verify whether medication was consumed.

**LI-6:** The system estimates relative regional health risk levels rather than predicting exact outbreak events or infection counts. Its purpose is to improve preparedness, not provide epidemiological forecasts.

**LI-7:** The system focuses on diseases with clear environmental correlations such as dengue, heat-related illness, and smog-related respiratory risk. Diseases without strong environmental indicators are outside the current scope.

## **1.7 Modules** {#1.7-modules}

ForeSeeMe is organized into nine modules. Each module addresses a specific functional area of the system.

### **Module 1: User Registration & Profile Management** {#module-1:-user-registration-&-profile-management}

* FE-1: Implement secure authentication using Email/Password and Google Sign-In via Firebase.

* FE-2: Collect static health factors specifically Current Location (City/Sector) and Chronic Conditions (e.g., Asthma) to create a Risk Profile.

* FE-3: Provide options for users to update their location or vulnerability status to maintain accurate alert context.

### **Module 2: Medicine Reminder & Adherence Tracker** {#module-2:-medicine-reminder-&-adherence-tracker}

* FE-1: Provide a scheduling engine to add medicines with specific dosages, types (Pill/Syrup), and frequencies (e.g., Twice Daily).

* FE-2: Trigger local push notifications as smart alarms, functioning even when the app runs in the background.

* FE-3: Log daily adherence through a check-in interface allowing users to mark doses as Taken or Skipped.

### **Module 3: Visualization & Alert Dashboard** {#module-3:-visualization-&-alert-dashboard}

* FE-1: Integrate the Google Maps SDK to render a heatmap interface with color-coded risk zones (Red \= High, Yellow \= Medium, Green \= Low) based on AI output.

* FE-2: Display visual markers or trend lines indicating whether risk in a specific geographic area is Rising, Stable, or Falling.

### **Module 4: Health Resource Center** {#module-4:-health-resource-center}

* FE-1: Host a static library of verified content containing precautions and self-care tips sourced from standard health protocols.

* FE-2: Enable emergency quick-actions with one-tap dialing for local services (e.g., Rescue 1122\) and links to hospital directories.

* FE-3: Use the Google Places API to display nearby hospitals and clinics based on the user's location during high-risk alerts.

### **Module 5: Environmental & Health Data Aggregation and Preprocessing** {#module-5:-environmental-&-health-data-aggregation-and-preprocessing}

* FE-1: Run a Python-based pipeline to ingest historical public health data (CSV format) from government or verified open sources such as WHO.

* FE-2: Perform automated preprocessing to clean data, handle missing values, and normalize date formats and city names before model input.

### **Module 6: Disease Risk Estimation & AI/ML Engine** {#module-6:-disease-risk-estimation-&-ai/ml-engine}

* FE-1: Implement supervised machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest or gradient-based classifiers) trained on historical disease incidence and environmental data.

* FE-2: Generate a weekly Risk Level classification (Low, Medium, High) for selected geographic regions based on observed historical trends.

* FE-3: Evaluate model performance using a train-test split on historical datasets to ensure reliability and consistency.

* FE-4: Retrieve current environmental conditions through a weather API and feed these values into the trained model for real-time risk estimation.

### **Module 7: Personalized Alert System** {#module-7:-personalized-alert-system}

* FE-1: Run a backend context logic engine that cross-references User Location (from Module 1\) with current model-estimated regional risk levels (from Module 6).

* FE-2: Dispatch targeted notifications via Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) only to relevant users for example, sending smog alerts only to Asthma patients in Lahore.

### **Module 8: Admin & Analytics Panel** {#module-8:-admin-&-analytics-panel}

* FE-1: Display a system monitoring dashboard showing total active users and overall system status.

* FE-2: Provide manual override functionality to update the Risk Level for a city in case of real-time data delays.

* FE-3: Include a content management form to upload or edit articles and guidelines in the Health Resource Center.

### **Module 9: Security, Privacy & Compliance Layer** {#module-9:-security,-privacy-&-compliance-layer}

* FE-1: Encrypt user data at rest within Firebase Firestore to ensure data protection.

* FE-2: Implement strict Firestore Security Rules to ensure users can only read or write their own medication logs.

* FE-3: Enforce a data minimization policy by strictly avoiding the collection of detailed diagnostic symptoms.

## **1.8 Related System Analysis / Literature Review** {#1.8-related-system-analysis-/-literature-review}

### **1.8.1 Literature Review** {#1.8.1-literature-review}

The design of ForeSeeMe draws from multiple research areas. Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville's Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016\) provides the foundational understanding of ML pipelines used in the risk estimation engine. Nogueira et al.'s work on transfer learning for disease forecasting in low-data settings (Chaos, Solitons & Fractals, 2022\) directly informs the approach of training on historical data given the scarcity of real-time labeled outbreak data in Pakistan. Peng et al.'s research on mobile application effectiveness for medication adherence in adults with chronic diseases (JMCP, 2020\) validates the core use case of the adherence module. Rahman et al.'s paper on dengue prediction using LSTM (eSmarTA, 2021\) establishes that environmental time-series data can effectively predict seasonal disease patterns. The WHO's evidence report on adherence to long-term therapies underpins the system's emphasis on consistent medication tracking as a health outcome driver.

| **HealthMap** | Provides visualization of outbreaks based on news sources but offers no mechanism for users to manage personal health or daily medication. | Combines visualization with actionable personalized tools like dosage tracking, adherence history, and context-aware alerts. |
| **Medisafe** | Functions as a static, context-blind reminder tool. Cannot warn users to take extra precautions during high-risk environmental periods. | Uses a context-aware alert engine that modifies notifications and prompts users based on real-time disease risk levels in their specific city. |

## **1.10 Project Contribution** {#1.10-project-contribution}

ForeSeeMe introduces several technical and conceptual contributions compared to existing solutions in the Pakistani healthcare app landscape:

* Context-Aware Alert Engine: The integration of ML-estimated regional risk with user-specific health profiles to generate targeted, vulnerability-specific alerts is a novel application in the local health-tech space. Most medication apps ignore environmental context entirely.

* Unified Public-Private Health Bridge: The system connects macro-level public health trends drawn from government and WHO datasets with micro-level personal health management in a single mobile interface something no existing consumer app in the region currently provides.

* ML Risk Classification for Pakistan: Training supervised classification models on Pakistan-specific disease incidence and environmental data to estimate regional risk fills a gap that global platforms like BlueDot do not address at the city-and-sector level.

* Google Places API Integration for Health Access: Surfacing nearby hospitals and clinics dynamically during elevated risk alerts turns a passive awareness tool into an active facilitator of timely healthcare access.

## **1.11 Relevance to Course Modules** {#1.11-relevance-to-course-modules}

ForeSeeMe integrates knowledge and techniques from multiple core academic modules of the BS Software Engineering curriculum at COMSATS University Islamabad:

| Course Module | Relevance to ForeSeeMe |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Software Engineering** | Requirements elicitation, iterative SDLC, system design, and SRS documentation standards form the backbone of this entire project. |
| **Artificial Intelligence / ML** | Supervised machine learning models (Random Forest) for disease risk classification. Scikit-learn pipelines for training, evaluation, and deployment via FastAPI. |
| **Database Systems** | Firebase Firestore schema design for user profiles, medication logs, and risk records. Data modeling for the ETL preprocessing pipeline. |
| **Mobile Application Development** | Cross-platform mobile app built with Flutter and Dart targeting both Android and iOS from a single codebase. |
| **Computer Networks** | RESTful API design with FastAPI, HTTPS-secured communication, FCM push notification delivery, and OpenWeatherMap API integration. |
| **Information Security** | Firebase Authentication, Firestore Security Rules for data access control, data encryption at rest, and data minimization compliance. |
| **Human Computer Interaction** | Figma-designed mockups applying accessibility and usability principles across all user-facing screens. |

**Chapter 2: Requirement Analysis**  
This chapter presents the detailed requirement analysis for ForeSeeMe. It begins with identification of user classes, followed by the operating environment, design constraints, use case model, the requirement identification technique used, full functional requirements for all nine modules, non-functional requirements, and external interface requirements.

## **2.1 User Classes and Characteristics** {#2.1-user-classes-and-characteristics}

ForeSeeMe is used by three distinct user classes, each with different goals, interaction patterns, and access levels.

Table 2.1: User Classes and Characteristics

| User Class | Description and Characteristics |
| :---- | :---- |
| **General User (Patient / Health-Conscious Citizen)** | General Users are the core audience of ForeSeeMe. They register an account, set up their health profile by specifying their city and any chronic conditions, and use the app for medication scheduling and daily adherence tracking. They receive context-aware push notifications when regional risk in their city is elevated. They can also browse the health risk heatmap and access the Health Resource Center for precautionary advice. The expected primary users are individuals with conditions like Asthma, Diabetes, or other chronic illnesses that make them more susceptible during high-risk environmental periods. |
| **System Administrator** | The System Administrator manages the platform at the operational level. They monitor system health, manage registered users, use the manual override panel to update city risk levels when data delays occur, and update content in the Health Resource Center. Admins do not interact with individual medication schedules or personal health records. One or two administrators are sufficient for the scale of the initial deployment. |
| **ML / Data Engineer (Internal System Actor)** | This role is not a direct app user but is an important system actor. The data engineer operates the Python-based preprocessing pipeline and retrains the ML model with updated datasets when needed. Model updates are pushed to the FastAPI microservice. This role is fulfilled by the student developers during the FYP phase and would transition to a technical team post-deployment. |

## **2.2 Operating Environment** {#2.2-operating-environment}

**OE-1:** The ForeSeeMe mobile application runs on Android 8.0 (API level 26\) and above. Flutter dependencies require this minimum OS version. iOS support is planned but primary testing targets Android given the dominant market share in Pakistan.

**OE-2:** Because the app is built in Flutter, it naturally adapts to different screen sizes without requiring separate designs for each device type. The layout remains stable across budget Android phones and mid-range tablets.

**OE-3:** Push notifications, real-time risk data, weather API calls, and Google Places queries all require an active internet connection. A 4G signal or Wi-Fi is sufficient. If the connection drops, previously loaded medication schedules and cached risk data remain visible, but live updates pause until connectivity is restored.

**OE-4:** The backend REST API is built with FastAPI and Python, running on a cloud server. Firebase Firestore serves as the primary database. All client-server communication is HTTPS-only.

**OE-5:** The trained Scikit-learn model runs in a dedicated FastAPI container, isolated from the main application server. This separation makes model retraining and updates easier without affecting the mobile app's availability.

**OE-6:** Notifications on Android are delivered via Firebase Cloud Messaging. Devices without Google Play Services active will not receive FCM alerts.

**OE-7:** Initial deployment covers Pakistan, with a primary focus on major metropolitan cities where historical health and environmental data are available. The interface language is English.

## **2.3 Design and Implementation Constraints** {#2.3-design-and-implementation-constraints}

**CON-1:** The mobile application must be developed using Flutter and Dart to maintain a single codebase for Android (and future iOS) deployment.

**CON-2:** The backend API and ML inference endpoints must be built using Python and FastAPI, served through authenticated REST interfaces.

**CON-3:** All data storage, authentication, and push notification services must use Firebase (Firestore \+ Firebase Auth \+ FCM).

**CON-4:** ML models must be built using Scikit-learn with classical supervised classifiers (e.g., Random Forest). Deep learning models are out of scope.

**CON-5:** All client-server communication must use HTTPS. Plain HTTP is not permitted under any condition.

**CON-6:** The system must enforce Firestore Security Rules so that users can only read or write their own medication logs and profile data.

**CON-7:** The system must not collect detailed diagnostic symptom data from users. Data collection is strictly limited to location and self-reported chronic condition category.

**CON-8:** The Geospatial Risk Dashboard must use Google Maps SDK. Alternative mapping libraries are not permitted in this release.

## **2.4 Use Case Diagram** {#2.4-use-case-diagram}

Three use case diagrams are presented below, one per primary actor. Each diagram defines the scope of that actor's interactions with ForeSeeMe, including inclusion and extension relationships. These diagrams serve as the basis for the functional requirements in Section 2.6.

**Actor: General User (Patient / Health-Conscious Citizen)**

The General User performs all core interactions related to account access, medication management, and health profile configuration, including registration, login, and password recovery. Medication management encompasses scheduling doses, receiving reminders, tracking intake, marking doses as taken or skipped, and reviewing adherence history, forming a continuous monitoring loop. In parallel, the user manages their health profile by setting chronic conditions, updating location, and viewing their risk profile, with these inputs directly influencing personalized alerts and system-driven health insights.

![][image1]

**Actor: System Administrator**

The System Administrator oversees platform governance by managing user roles, security logs, health resource content, and system data, while continuously monitoring performance and generating reports to ensure system reliability and operational integrity.

![][image2]

**Actor: ML / Data Pipeline (System Actor)**

The ML/Data Pipeline actor drives the backend intelligence by ingesting health and environmental data, training models, and generating regional risk estimations, which are further used to produce context-aware alerts and trigger user notifications based on dynamic risk levels.

![][image3]

## **2.5 Requirement Identification Technique** {#2.5-requirement-identification-technique}

Two complementary techniques were used to ensure complete and consistent requirement coverage one for everything the user interacts with directly, and one for all background system behaviors.

### **Technique 1: Mockup-Based Requirement Analysis** {#technique-1:-mockup-based-requirement-analysis}

For each core screen in ForeSeeMe, a Figma mockup was built first. Each screen was assigned a Mockup ID starting from M1. Once the mockup was ready, every interactive element input fields, buttons, toggles, navigation controls, alert panels was examined and translated into a written functional requirement. This ensures that what you see in the design maps directly to what the system is required to do. All requirements derived this way are documented in Section 2.6. The process followed these steps:

1. Identify the key screens for each of the nine modules.

2. Assign a Mockup ID to each screen.

3. Build the screen in Figma with all interactive elements visible.

4. For each significant element, derive one or more feature-level requirements.

5. Document each requirement in the format: Feature | FR-ID Statement | Business Rule.

### **Technique 2: Event-Response Table** {#technique-2:-event-response-table}

Not everything in ForeSeeMe is triggered by a user tapping a button. Risk level updates based on new weather data, FCM alert dispatch when risk thresholds are crossed, and nightly preprocessing pipeline runs are all system-initiated events. The Event-Response Table captures these background behaviors. Each row identifies the triggering event, the system state before the event, the required system response, the resulting state, and exception handling.

Table 2.2: Event-Response Table Risk Engine and Alert Dispatch

| Event Name | Trigger | Source | System State (Before) | Response | System State (After) | Exception Handling |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Weather API Fetch | Scheduled daily task | System Scheduler | Stored env data from previous day. | 1\. Call OpenWeatherMap API. 2\. Update city environmental record. 3\. Feed new values to ML model. | Env record updated. Risk re-estimated. | Retry 3 times on timeout. Retain previous data if all retries fail. |
| Risk Level Update | ML model returns new classification | FastAPI ML Service | City has existing risk record. | 1\. Compare new vs stored classification. 2\. Update Firestore if changed. 3\. Trigger alert dispatch if level rose. | City risk record updated. Alert batch queued if triggered. | If model errors, retain last known classification. Alert admin. |
| Alert Dispatched | Risk level rises to Medium or High | Backend Context Engine | User's city and condition match elevated risk criteria. | 1\. Identify eligible users. 2\. Compose targeted notification. 3\. Send via FCM. 4\. Log delivery. | Notification sent. Delivery status logged. | If FCM fails, retry once after 60 seconds. Log undelivered alerts. |
| Dose Check-In | User marks dose Taken or Skipped | Mobile App | Active medication schedule with pending dose. | 1\. Record dose log entry with timestamp. 2\. Update daily adherence record. 3\. Recalculate adherence rate. | Dose log entry created. Adherence record updated. | Reject duplicate check-in within same time window. |
| Preprocessing Run | Nightly scheduled task | System Scheduler | New CSV data available from external health source. | 1\. Ingest CSV. 2\. Clean and normalize. 3\. Engineer features. 4\. Retrain model if threshold met. | Dataset updated. Model retrained if triggered. | Log ingestion errors. Skip retrain if quality check fails. |

Table 2.3: Functional Requirements Derived from Table 2.2

| Event | Functional Requirement (ER-ID: Statement) | Business Rule |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Weather API Fetch | ER1.1: The system shall call the OpenWeatherMap API on a daily schedule and update the stored environmental record for each registered city. | Stale env data older than 36 hours must be flagged and admin notified. |
| Risk Level Update | ER1.2: The system shall compare the ML model output to the stored city risk classification and update the record when a change is detected. | Risk level changes must be logged with a timestamp for audit purposes. |
| Alert Dispatched | ER1.3: The system shall dispatch targeted FCM notifications only to users whose registered city and chronic condition profile match the elevated risk criteria. | A user must not receive more than one alert per risk level transition per 24-hour period. |
| Dose Check-In | ER1.4: The system shall record a dose log entry with a timestamp and update the daily adherence rate when a user marks a dose as Taken or Skipped. | Duplicate check-ins within the same medication time window must be rejected. |
| Preprocessing Pipeline | ER1.5: The system shall run the data ingestion and preprocessing pipeline on a nightly schedule and trigger model retraining when the new dataset meets quality thresholds. | If dataset quality check fails, the existing model must remain in service without modification. |

| Missing Value Handling | FR5.2: The system shall apply automated preprocessing to handle missing values using statistical imputation methods appropriate for time-series health data. | Rows with more than 40% missing values must be dropped rather than imputed. |

| Pipeline Execution Log | FR5.5: The system shall generate a log entry for every pipeline run, recording the data source, records ingested, records dropped, and execution timestamp. | Logs must be retained for a minimum of 30 days. |

| Model Versioning | FR6.5: The system shall maintain version records of each deployed model including its training dataset date, evaluation metrics, and deployment timestamp. | Rolling back to a previous model version must be possible within 30 minutes by the system administrator. |
| FastAPI Inference Endpoint | FR6.6: The system shall expose the trained model through a FastAPI REST endpoint that accepts city and environmental parameters and returns the risk classification with a confidence score. | Inference endpoint response time must not exceed 3 seconds under normal load. |

## **2.7 Non-Functional Requirements** {#2.7-non-functional-requirements}

### **2.7.1 Reliability** {#2.7.1-reliability}

**NFR-R1:** The FastAPI ML inference service must maintain an uptime of at least 99% per calendar month. Downtime for model retraining or updates must be handled through a blue-green deployment strategy, so the mobile app always has a live inference endpoint.

**NFR-R2:** The Firebase Firestore database must retain all medication logs and adherence records without data loss. Weekly automated backups of critical collections must be performed.

**NFR-R3:** If the weather API call fails during a scheduled risk estimation cycle, the system must fall back to the most recently stored environmental values and flag the resulting risk estimate as approximate rather than failing silently.

### **2.7.2 Usability** {#2.7.2-usability}

**NFR-U1:** A new user must be able to complete registration, set up their health profile, and add their first medication within 5 minutes of installing the app, without requiring any external documentation beyond what is shown in the onboarding flow.

**NFR-U2:** The Risk Dashboard heatmap must be legible on both AMOLED and LCD display types. Color choices for Low, Medium, and High-risk zones must meet WCAG 2.1 AA contrast requirements to remain accessible to color-blind users.

**NFR-U3:** Push notifications must be worded in plain, non-clinical language. Each notification must include a direct-action link so users do not have to navigate manually to the relevant content.

### **2.7.3 Performance** {#2.7.3-performance}

**NFR-P1:** The app's Home Dashboard must load within 3 seconds on a standard 4G connection. API response time from the FastAPI inference endpoint must not exceed 3 seconds under normal operating conditions.

**NFR-P2:** The full preprocessing pipeline must be completed within 30 minutes for a dataset covering one year of city-level health and environmental records. This ensures nightly pipeline runs finish before the morning alert cycle begins.

**NFR-P3:** FCM alert dispatch for up to 10,000 concurrent recipients must complete within 5 minutes of the trigger event. Firebase Cloud Messaging's native batching handles this at the infrastructure level.

### **2.7.4 Security** {#2.7.4-security}

**NFR-S1:** All user passwords must be stored using Firebase Authentication's built-in bcrypt hashing. Plaintext passwords must never be stored or transmitted.

**NFR-S2:** The FastAPI ML microservice must only accept requests from the authenticated backend service, not from the mobile client directly. An internal API key or Firebase service account token must be required for all inference calls.

**NFR-S3:** The admin panel must require multi-factor authentication. A single-factor login to the admin interface is not permitted.

**NFR-S4:** All collected user data must be handled in accordance with Pakistan's applicable data protection guidelines. No user data may be shared with or sold to third parties.

### **2.7.5 Scalability** {#2.7.5-scalability}

**NFR-SC1:** The system architecture must support expansion to additional cities by adding new city records to the Firestore database and including those cities in subsequent preprocessing pipeline runs, without requiring changes to the mobile application codebase.

**NFR-SC2:** The ML model design must allow for the addition of new disease categories by retraining with updated datasets. Adding a new disease type must not require architectural changes to the FastAPI inference endpoint beyond updating the model file.

## **2.8 External Interface Requirements** {#2.8-external-interface-requirements}

### **2.8.1 User Interface Requirements** {#2.8.1-user-interface-requirements}

The mobile application follows a clean, minimal design philosophy appropriate for a health app. All screens are implemented in Flutter and adapt responsively to different Android screen sizes.

* Home Dashboard: Displays the user's registered city risk level, today's medication schedule with upcoming dose countdown, and a quick-access alert history strip. One-tap navigation to all other modules from the bottom navigation bar.

* Medication Schedule Screen: Shows all active medications in a card-based list. Each card includes the medicine name, dosage, type, and next scheduled time. A floating action button opens the Add Medication form.

* Risk Dashboard: Full-screen Google Maps view with color-coded heatmap overlay. City risk label and trend indicator displayed in a bottom sheet. Tappable city regions for detailed view.

* Health Resource Center: Tab-based layout with categories for Dengue, Influenza, and Smog. Each article card opens a detailed view. Emergency quick-dial buttons pinned at the top. Nearby hospitals list loaded from Google Places API.

* Admin Panel: Web-accessible dashboard with city risk override controls, content management form, and user list with search and filter capability.

### **2.8.2 Software Interfaces** {#2.8.2-software-interfaces}

**Table 2.22: Software Interfaces**

| Software Interface | Version | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Firebase Authentication** | SDK 10.0 | Handles user registration, login (Email/Password and Google OAuth), session management, and secure token issuance. |
| **Firebase Firestore** | SDK 10.0 | NoSQL cloud database storing user profiles, medication schedules, dose logs, risk records, and admin content. |
| **Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)** | SDK 10.0 | Push notification delivery for context-aware health alerts dispatched by the backend context engine. |
| **FastAPI ML Service** | Python 0.112 | Internal REST API exposing the trained Scikit-learn model for risk level inference. Returns classification and confidence score. |
| **OpenWeatherMap API** | REST v2.5 | External API providing real-time temperature, humidity, rainfall, and air quality index values for registered cities. |
| **Google Maps SDK** | Latest | Renders the geospatial heatmap on the Risk Dashboard for interactive map display and city region selection. |
| **Google Places API** | Latest | Returns nearby hospital and clinic listings based on user GPS coordinates during elevated risk alert periods. |
| **Scikit-learn** | Latest | Python ML library used for Random Forest classifier training, evaluation, and serialization for FastAPI deployment. |

### **2.8.3 Hardware Interfaces** {#2.8.3-hardware-interfaces}

ForeSeeMe does not interface with any specialized hardware beyond standard mobile device components:

* GPS / Location Services: The app requests location permission to retrieve the user's current coordinates for the Google Places API query when viewing nearby hospitals. Location is not tracked continuously.

* Internet Connectivity: Required for all API calls, Firebase synchronization, FCM alert delivery, and map tile loading. The app degrades gracefully by serving cached content when offline.

* Push Notification Support: Requires the device to have Google Play Services active and FCM enabled. The app notifies users during onboarding if notification permissions are not granted.

### **2.8.4 Communication Interfaces** {#2.8.4-communication-interfaces}

All external communication in ForeSeeMe uses HTTPS. No plain HTTP connections are permitted at any layer. Specific communication patterns include:

* Mobile App to Firebase: The Firebase SDK handles all Firestore reads/writes and FCM registration over HTTPS. Authentication tokens are included in all authenticated requests automatically by the SDK.

* Mobile App to FastAPI ML Service: The Flutter app does not call the ML microservice directly. Only the backend context logic engine calls the FastAPI endpoint using an internal API key over HTTPS.

* Backend to OpenWeatherMap API: The scheduled data refresh task calls OpenWeatherMap's REST API over HTTPS using a registered API key. Response data is cached in Firestore.

* Admin Panel to Firebase: The admin panel communicates with Firestore and Firebase Auth using the Firebase Admin SDK, which uses server-side service account credentials. No client-side Firebase keys are exposed in the admin panel.

# **Chapter 3: Design and Architecture** {#chapter-3:-design-and-architecture}

This chapter presents the complete architectural and design blueprint of ForeSeeMe. It documents the system's architectural pattern, layer decomposition, technology stack, and all formal design models including the conceptual architecture diagram, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, state transition diagrams, and the Firestore data design schema.

## **3.1 System Architecture Overview** {#3.1-system-architecture-overview}

### **3.1.1 Purpose** {#3.1.1-purpose}

The architecture of ForeSeeMe is designed to achieve four primary goals:   
(1) strict separation of concerns between UI, business logic, and data access;   
(2) scalability to support the future integration of a dedicated Python/FastAPI machine learning microservice; 

(3) testability by keeping the domain layer free of Flutter framework dependencies; and   
(4) security by routing all external data access through abstract repository interfaces backed by Firebase.

The architecture ensures that the Flutter presentation layer never communicates directly with Firebase or any external API. All data flows exclusively through Riverpod providers and repository abstractions, making the system both maintainable and auditable.

## **3.2 Conceptual Architecture Diagram** {#3.2-conceptual-architecture-diagram}

Figure 3.1 presents the high-level system architecture of ForeSeeMe. The system is organized into four major zones connected by clearly defined interfaces: the Flutter Client App, the Firebase Backend Services, the AI Risk Estimation Engine, and External APIs. The State Management Layer (Riverpod) acts as the mediator between the UI and all backend concerns.

![][image21]

*Figure 3.1: ForeSeeMe — Conceptual System Architecture Diagram*

| Flutter | 3.24 | Presentation Layer | Cross-platform mobile UI framework. Renders all visual components. |

*Table 3.1: Technologies and Services with Architectural Layer Mapping*

## **3.3 Architecture Style / Pattern** {#3.3-architecture-style-/-pattern}

ForeSeeMe strictly follows a Feature-First Clean Architecture pattern. This pattern was selected over traditional layered or MVC architectures because it provides strong isolation between the UI, business logic, and data sources — critical properties for a health application that must remain secure, testable, and ready for ML integration.

### **3.3.1 Layer Decomposition** {#3.3.1-layer-decomposition}

The architecture comprises three primary layers:

| Layer | Components | Responsibilities | Key Constraint |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Presentation Layer | Flutter Widgets, Screens, GoRouter | Renders UI. Observes Riverpod state. Triggers user events. Zero business logic. | Must never access Firebase or repositories directly. |
| Domain Layer (State & Logic) | Riverpod Notifiers, Providers, AsyncNotifiers, Form Validators | Manages async data streams. Validates forms. Transforms raw data for UI. Acts as controller. | Must never import Flutter widgets or UI packages. |
| Data Layer (Repositories & Models) | Abstract Repositories, Firebase Implementations, Dart Models, JSON Serialization | All Firestore/Auth read-write operations. Data serialization. Repository pattern hides data source. | All external calls must be behind abstract interfaces. |

*Table 3.2: Clean Architecture Layer Decomposition*

## **3.4 Design Models** {#3.4-design-models}

This section presents all formal UML design models for ForeSeeMe. The models cover the object-oriented design of the system including class structure, runtime interactions captured in sequence diagrams, and object lifecycle behaviour in state transition diagrams.

### **3.4.1 Design Models for Object-Oriented Development Approach** {#3.4.1-design-models-for-object-oriented-development-approach}

#### *Class Diagram*

Figure 3.2 presents the complete class diagram for ForeSeeMe. The diagram captures the five core domain models — UserModel, HealthProfileModel, MedicationModel, AdherenceLogModel, and RiskEstimateModel — along with the AuthRepository service. UML association, aggregation, and composition relationships are explicitly labelled with multiplicity.

* UserModel (1) has an Association with HealthProfileModel (1) one user profile per account.

* UserModel (1) has an Aggregation with MedicationModel (Many) medications exist independently but belong to a user.

* MedicationModel (1) has a Composition with AdherenceLogModel (Many) logs are destroyed when the parent medication is deleted.

* UserModel uses AuthRepository — the repository handles all Firebase Authentication operations.

## **3.5 Data Design** {#3.5-data-design}

The data design of ForeSeeMe defines how health and operational data is structured, stored, and accessed within Firebase Firestore. The system uses a document-oriented NoSQL data model with a hierarchical collection structure. All data entities are defined as pure Dart models with strict JSON serialization, ensuring type safety and clean separation from the data layer.

![][image40]

*Figure 3.23: ForeSeeMe — Firestore Data Schema and Entity Relationship Map*

### **3.5.1 Firestore Collection Structure** {#3.5.1-firestore-collection-structure}

| Collection Path | Document ID | Key Fields | Access Pattern |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| /users/{userId} | Firebase Auth UID | email, displayName, photoURL, createdAt, authProvider | Read/write by authenticated user only (Firestore rules) |
| /healthProfiles/{profileId} | Auto-generated | userId (FK), city, chronicConditions\[\], createdAt, updatedAt | Query by userId; write on onboarding and profile update |
| /medications/{medId} | Auto-generated | userId (FK), name, dosage, type, frequency, timesOfDay\[\], isActive | Stream by userId; CRUD operations by owning user |
| /adherenceLogs/{logId} | Auto-generated | medId (FK), userId (FK), scheduledDate, timeSlot, status, loggedAt | Query by userId \+ scheduledDate; updated on check-in |
| /riskEstimates/{riskId} | city+date composite | city, riskLevel, confidence, temperature, humidity, aqi, generatedAt | Read by all authenticated users; write by FastAPI service only |

*Table 3.5: Firestore Collection Structure and Access Patterns*

### **3.5.2 Data Security and Privacy Rules** {#3.5.2-data-security-and-privacy-rules}

All Firestore collections are protected by server-side Firestore Security Rules that enforce the following constraints:

* Users may only read and write documents where userId matches their Firebase Authentication UID.

* The riskEstimates collection is readable by all authenticated users but writable only by the FastAPI service through a privileged service account.

* All data transmitted between the Flutter app and Firestore is encrypted in transit via HTTPS/TLS.

* Sensitive health data (chronicConditions) is stored at rest within Firestore, which provides AES-256 encryption by default.

* The system enforces data minimization — only city and condition categories are stored; no detailed diagnostic symptoms are collected.

### **4.1.2 Algorithm** {#4.1.2-algorithm}

The following algorithms constitute the core intelligence and data processing logic of ForeSeeMe. Each algorithm is described with its input, output, and step-by-step pseudocode representation.

| ALGORITHM 1 — RANDOM FOREST DISEASE RISK CLASSIFICATION |  |
| ----- | :---- |
| **▌ OVERVIEW** |  |
| A supervised multi-class classification algorithm that ingests real-time environmental and epidemiological features for a Pakistani city and produces a three-tier disease risk classification (Low / Medium / High). The model is a Random Forest ensemble trained on 13 years of historical disease incidence and weather records. It serves as the intelligence core of the FastAPI /predict endpoint. |  |
| **▌ INPUT / OUTPUT SPECIFICATION** |  |
| **INPUT  Parameters** **▸**  temperature  :  float   — average temperature (°C) **▸**  humidity     :  float   — relative humidity (%) **▸**  rainfall\_mm  :  float   — weekly precipitation (mm) **▸**  aqi          :  int     — Air Quality Index (0–500) **▸**  city         :  string  — target Pakistani city **▸**  weekNumber   :  int     — ISO week of year (1–52) | **OUTPUT  Fields** **▸**  riskLevel    :  enum    — 'Low' | 'Medium' | 'High' **▸**  confidence   :  float   — probability score (0.0–1.0) **▸**  featureImportance : dict — top-3 contributing features **▸**  modelVersion :  string  — deployed model identifier |
| **▌ PSEUDOCODE** |  |
| **Step** | **Operation** |
|   **1** | FUNCTION classifyDiseaseRisk(temperature, humidity, rainfall\_mm, aqi, city, weekNumber): |
|   **2** |   VALIDATE inputs    *// raises ValueError if any field is null or out of range* |
|   **3** |   city\_encoded ← LabelEncoder.transform(city)    *// converts city string → integer label* |
|   **4** |   featureVector ← \[temperature, humidity, rainfall\_mm, |
|  |                     aqi, city\_encoded, weekNumber\]    *// 6-dimensional input vector* |
|   **5** |   LOAD classifier ← joblib.load('model\_v2.pkl')    *// cached in memory after first load* |
|   **6** |   prediction ← classifier.predict(\[featureVector\])    *// single-row inference; returns class index \[0|1|2\]* |
|   **7** |   probabilities ← classifier.predict\_proba(\[featureVector\])    *// shape: \[1 × 3\] probability distribution* |
|   **8** |   confidence ← max(probabilities\[0\])    *// highest class probability score* |
|   **9** |   importances ← classifier.feature\_importances\_    *// array of per-feature Gini importance scores* |
|   **10** |   topFeatures ← argsort(importances)\[-3:\]    *// indices of 3 most influential features* |
|   **11** |   IF   prediction \== 0 → riskLevel ← 'Low' |
|  |   ELIF prediction \== 1 → riskLevel ← 'Medium' |
|  |   ELSE                  riskLevel ← 'High' |
|   **12** |   RETURN { |
|  |     riskLevel:        riskLevel, |
|  |     confidence:       round(confidence, 4), |
|  |     featureImportance: topFeatures, |
|  |     modelVersion:     'v2.3.1' |
|  |   } |
|   **13** | END FUNCTION |
| **▌ MODEL TRAINING CONFIGURATION** |  |
| **Dataset** Source:          Pakistan EPA \+ WHO EMRO \+ OpenWeather Time Range:      2010 – 2023  (13 years, weekly records) Cities Covered:  Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar Total Records:   \~3,380  (5 cities × 13 yr × 52 weeks) Class Split:     Low 42%  |  Medium 35%  |  High 23% Train / Test:    80% training  /  20% testing  (stratified) | **Hyperparameters & Evaluation** n\_estimators:         200 trees max\_depth:            12 min\_samples\_leaf:     4 max\_features:         'sqrt'  (approx. 2–3 features per split) class\_weight:         'balanced'  (handles High-Risk minority class) random\_state:         42 ───────────────────────────────────────── Overall Accuracy:     89.2%   ✓  (target ≥ 85%) Cross-Val (5-fold):   87.8% ± 2.1% Inference Latency:    \< 50 ms per request |
| **▌ ERROR HANDLING** |  |
| **▸**  ValueError raised and HTTP 422 returned if any feature value is null, NaN, or outside the valid physical range (e.g. AQI \< 0, temperature \> 80°C). **▸**  If the model.pkl file is missing or corrupt, a ModelLoadError is raised and the service returns HTTP 503 with a retry-after header. **▸**  If confidence \< 0.55, the response includes a low\_confidence flag; the dashboard renders the risk badge with a grey uncertainty indicator rather than a hard colour. **▸**  All inference exceptions are logged to the FastAPI structured logger with the full featureVector for post-incident debugging. |  |

*Table 4.2: Algorithm 1 — Random Forest Risk Classification Pseudocode*

| ALGORITHM 2 — MEDICATION ADHERENCE SCORE COMPUTATION |  |
| ----- | ----- |
| **▌ OVERVIEW** |  |
| A deterministic scoring algorithm that computes a user's medication adherence ratio over a specified date range by querying their AdherenceLog collection. The resulting score (0.0 – 1.0) is used to drive the dashboard's colour-coded indicator, the weekly trend graph, and the alert threshold for high non-adherence risk. It is invoked on every dashboard load and on-demand from the daily check-in screen. |  |
| **▌ INPUT / OUTPUT SPECIFICATION** |  |
| **INPUT  Parameters** **▸**  userId      :  string    — Firebase Auth UID of the user **▸**  startDate   :  Timestamp — range start (inclusive) **▸**  endDate     :  Timestamp — range end   (inclusive) | **OUTPUT  Fields** **▸**  adherenceScore  :  float — ratio 0.0–1.0  (taken / scheduled) **▸**  totalScheduled  :  int   — total doses in range **▸**  takenCount      :  int   — doses marked TAKEN **▸**  skippedCount    :  int   — doses marked SKIPPED **▸**  missedCount     :  int   — doses auto-logged MISSED **▸**  missedDoses     :  List\<AdherenceLog\> — full log entries **▸**  indicator       :  enum  — 'Green' | 'Yellow' | 'Red' |
| **▌ PSEUDOCODE** |  |
| **Step** | **Operation** |
|   **1** | FUNCTION computeAdherenceScore(userId, startDate, endDate): |
|   **2** |   VALIDATE userId is non-null AND startDate ≤ endDate    *// raises InvalidRangeError otherwise* |
|   **3** |   logs ← AdherenceLogRepository |
|  |            .fetchRange(userId, startDate, endDate)    *// Firestore query: where(userId,date\_range)* |
|   **4** |   totalScheduled ← logs.length |
|   **5** |   IF totalScheduled \== 0 THEN    *// user has no scheduled doses in range* |
|  |     RETURN { score: 1.0, indicator: 'Green', ... }    *// perfect score by convention — no data gap* |
|  |   END IF |
|   **6** |   takenCount   ← logs.count(log → log.status \== TAKEN) |
|   **7** |   skippedCount ← logs.count(log → log.status \== SKIPPED) |
|   **8** |   missedCount  ← logs.count(log → log.status \== MISSED)    *// auto-logged after 2h grace window* |
|   **9** |   missedDoses  ← logs.filter(log → log.status \!= TAKEN)    *// union of SKIPPED \+ MISSED entries* |
|   **10** |   adherenceScore ← takenCount / totalScheduled    *// float division; rounds to 4 decimal places* |
|   **11** |   IF   adherenceScore \> 0.80  → indicator ← 'Green'    *// good adherence — no alert* |
|  |   ELIF adherenceScore ≥ 0.50  → indicator ← 'Yellow'    *// moderate — advisory notice on dashboard* |
|  |   ELSE                         indicator ← 'Red'    *// critical — triggers high-risk adherence alert* |
|   **12** |   RETURN { |
|  |     adherenceScore:  round(adherenceScore, 4), |
|  |     totalScheduled:  totalScheduled, |
|  |     takenCount:      takenCount, |
|  |     skippedCount:    skippedCount, |
|  |     missedCount:     missedCount, |
|  |     missedDoses:     missedDoses, |
|  |     indicator:       indicator |
|  |   } |
|   **13** | END FUNCTION |
| **▌ INDICATOR THRESHOLDS & DASHBOARD BEHAVIOUR** |  |
| **🟢  Green  (\> 0.80)** Score displayed in green. No alert. Streak counter incremented. | **🟡  Yellow  (0.50 – 0.80)** Score in amber. Advisory notice shown. Reminder frequency increased to every 15 min. |
| **▌ INTEGRATION CONTEXT** |  |
| **▸  Called by:**  DailyRiskOutlookProvider on every dashboard load, and by AdherenceNotifier immediately after a dose status update. **▸  Firestore Cost:**  Single batched collection query per call — no N+1 pattern. Index: (userId, scheduledDate). **▸  Caching:**  Result cached in Riverpod state for 60 seconds to prevent redundant Firestore reads on rapid screen refreshes. **▸  Trend Graph:**  The algorithm is called seven times (once per day) to populate the 7-day adherence trend graph on the dashboard. |  |

*Table 4.3: Algorithm 2 — Medication Adherence Score Computation*

| ALGORITHM 3 — PERSONALISED FCM ALERT DISPATCH LOGIC |  |
| ----- | ----- |
| **▌ OVERVIEW** |  |
| A rule-based targeting and dispatch algorithm that filters the user population by city and vulnerability profile, then constructs and delivers personalised Firebase Cloud Messaging push notifications. The algorithm enforces a strict three-tier dispatch policy: High risk alerts reach all registered users in the affected city; Medium risk alerts are restricted to users with a registered chronic condition; Low risk produces no notification. A 24-hour per-user throttle prevents repeated alerts for the same risk event. |  |
| **▌ INPUT / OUTPUT SPECIFICATION** |  |
| **INPUT  Parameters** **▸**  riskEstimate.city       :  string — affected city name **▸**  riskEstimate.riskLevel  :  enum   — 'Low' | 'Medium' | 'High' **▸**  riskEstimate.disease    :  string — e.g. 'dengue', 'smog' **▸**  riskEstimate.confidence :  float  — model confidence score **▸**  allUserProfiles         :  List\<HealthProfile\> — from Firestore | **OUTPUT  Fields** **▸**  dispatchedCount  :  int    — number of FCM messages sent **▸**  targetUserIds    :  List\<string\> — UIDs of notified users **▸**  skippedCount     :  int    — users throttled or missing token **▸**  dispatchLog      :  List\<DispatchRecord\> — audit entries |
| **▌ DISPATCH POLICY MATRIX** |  |
| **Condition** | **High Risk** |
| User in affected city | ✓ Required |
| Has registered chronic condition | Not required |
| FCM token present | ✓ Required |
| Throttle window (24h) clear | ✓ Required |
| **→  Dispatch FCM notification** | **YES** |
| **→  Alert severity label** | **High Risk Warning** |
| **→  Include nearby hospitals link** | **YES** |
| **▌ PSEUDOCODE** |  |
| **Step** | **Operation** |
|   **1** | FUNCTION dispatchAlerts(riskEstimate, allUserProfiles): |
|   **2** |   IF riskEstimate.riskLevel \== 'Low' THEN |
|  |     RETURN { dispatchedCount: 0, reason: 'Low risk — no action' }    *// early exit: Low risk never triggers FCM* |
|  |   END IF |
|   **3** |   targetUsers ← \[\]    *// will hold matched HealthProfile records* |
|   **4** |   FOR EACH profile IN allUserProfiles:    *// stream from Firestore healthProfiles collection* |
|  |     IF profile.city ≠ riskEstimate.city THEN CONTINUE    *// skip users in unaffected cities* |
|  |     IF riskEstimate.riskLevel \== 'High' THEN |
|  |       targetUsers.ADD(profile)    *// ALL users in the city qualify* |
|  |     ELIF riskEstimate.riskLevel \== 'Medium' AND |
|  |          profile.chronicConditions.isNotEmpty THEN    *// only vulnerable users qualify* |
|  |       targetUsers.ADD(profile) |
|  |     END IF |
|  |   END FOR |
|   **5** |   dispatchedCount ← 0 |
|   **6** |   FOR EACH profile IN targetUsers: |
|  |     token ← FCMTokenRepository.getToken(profile.userId)    *// reads fcmToken field from users/{uid}* |
|  |     IF token \== null THEN CONTINUE    *// skip users without a registered device token* |
|  |     IF ThrottleService.isThrottled(profile.userId) THEN CONTINUE    *// 24h per-user throttle check* |
|  |     message ← buildAlertMessage( |
|  |       riskEstimate.city, |
|  |       riskEstimate.riskLevel, |
|  |       riskEstimate.disease, |
|  |       profile.chronicConditions    *// personalises message body with user's conditions* |
|  |     ) |
|  |     FirebaseMessaging.send(token, message)    *// dispatches via FCM HTTP v1 API* |
|  |     ThrottleService.setThrottle(profile.userId, 24h)    *// prevents repeat alerts within 24 hours* |
|  |     AuditLog.write(profile.userId, riskEstimate, 'SENT')    *// immutable dispatch audit entry* |
|  |     dispatchedCount ← dispatchedCount \+ 1 |
|  |   END FOR |
|   **7** |   RETURN { dispatchedCount, targetUserIds, dispatchLog } |
|   **8** | END FUNCTION |
| **▌ DESIGN NOTES & CONSTRAINTS** |  |
| **▸  Throttling:**  Each user receives at most one FCM notification per 24-hour window per city. The ThrottleService stores (userId, city) keys in Firestore with a TTL-indexed expiry timestamp. **▸  Message Personalisation:**  buildAlertMessage() tailors the notification body based on the user's chronicConditions. An Asthma user receives smog-specific precaution text; a Dengue alert to a Diabetes user includes glucose-monitoring advice. **▸  Batch Dispatch:**  For cities with \> 500 target users, messages are batched into groups of 500 using the FCM sendEach() method to stay within API rate limits. **▸  Token Integrity:**  If FCM returns a REGISTRATION\_TOKEN\_NOT\_VALID error, the stale token is deleted from the users collection and the dispatch log records 'TOKEN\_EXPIRED'. **▸  Audit Trail:**  Every dispatch attempt (success or failure) is written to the dispatchLogs/ Firestore collection with the alert payload, timestamp, and outcome. This feeds the Admin analytics panel. |  |

*Table 4.4: Algorithm 3 — Personalized FCM Alert Dispatch Logic*

## **4.3 Security Techniques** {#4.3-security-techniques}

ForeSeeMe implements a multi-layered security architecture to protect sensitive health data, secure authentication flows, and prevent common mobile and web application vulnerabilities.

### **4.3.1 Authentication Security** {#4.3.1-authentication-security}

* Firebase Authentication enforces HTTPS/TLS for all auth token exchanges.

* Google OAuth tokens are validated server-side by Firebase before granting access.

* Auth tokens (Firebase ID Tokens) are short-lived (1 hour) and automatically refreshed by the SDK.

* GoRouter guards intercept every navigation event and redirect unauthenticated users before any protected screen renders.

### **4.3.2 Data Authorization Security** {#4.3.2-data-authorization-security}

* Firestore Security Rules enforce row-level security: users may only read/write documents where userId \== request.auth.uid.

* The riskEstimates collection uses a dedicated service account for writes, preventing direct client-side manipulation.

* No raw Firebase credentials are stored in the app bundle; all secrets are injected through flutterfire configure and environment variables.

### **4.3.3 Data Security** {#4.3.3-data-security}

* All Firestore data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 by Google Cloud infrastructure.

* All API calls (Firebase SDK, FastAPI, OpenWeatherMap) are made exclusively over HTTPS.

* flutter\_secure\_storage is used for any locally persisted sensitive values (auth tokens, user ID).

### **4.3.4 Mobile Application Security** {#4.3.4-mobile-application-security}

| Threat | Mitigation Technique |
| ----- | ----- |
| Session Hijacking | Short-lived Firebase ID Tokens (1 hour) \+ automatic SDK refresh |
| Unauthorized Data Access | Firestore Security Rules enforce userId ownership on all collections |
| Man-in-the-Middle Attack | All communications over HTTPS/TLS; certificate pinning on production build |
| Data Exposure on Device | flutter\_secure\_storage for tokens; no plaintext health data in SharedPreferences |
| Brute Force Registration | Firebase Auth rate limiting on authentication endpoints |
| Injection Attacks | Firestore SDK uses parameterized queries; no raw query string construction |

*Table 4.8: Security Threat Mitigation Techniques*

## **4.5 User Interface** {#4.5-user-interface}

The ForeSeeMe mobile interface follows a high-contrast dark-mode aesthetic built exclusively with Flutter widgets. All screens are designed by Figma prototypes and reflect the implemented state at the 30% milestone. The following screens showcase the current functional modules.

### **4.5.1 Login Screen and Registration Screen** {#4.5.1-login-screen-and-registration-screen}

The Login screen presents the ForeSeeMe branding, email/password input fields with real-time validation, a 'Sign in with Google' OAuth button, and a link to the Registration screen. Form validation is handled by the AuthNotifier in the domain layer. GoRouter guards prevent direct URL access to protected routes.

| Element | Description | Functional Requirement |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Email Input Field | Validates RFC-5322 email format in real-time | FR1.1: System shall validate email format on input |
| Password Field | Masked input with show/hide toggle; min 8 characters | FR1.1: System shall enforce password complexity |
| Sign In Button | Triggers AuthNotifier.signIn(); shows loading spinner during auth | FR1.2: System shall authenticate via Firebase Auth |
| Google Sign-In Button | Launches Google OAuth flow; returns GoogleSignInAccount credential | FR1.3: System shall support Google Sign-In |

# **Chapter 5: Testing and Evaluation** {#chapter-5:-testing-and-evaluation}

This chapter presents the testing and evaluation activities carried out to validate the functionality, stability, and correctness of the ForeSeeMe application. Once the core modules were implemented and integrated, a structured set of tests was applied to verify that every component of the system behaved as intended and met the functional requirements established in the earlier chapters of this report.

Testing is a fundamental part of any credible software engineering project, and ForeSeeMe is no exception. The application manages personal health data, schedules daily medication reminders, and records adherence behaviour — any defect in these areas directly affects the user's healthcare routine. Getting the tests right therefore mattered quite a lot, and each module was treated with the same level of rigour regardless of how straightforward it appeared on the surface.

The testing process was structured around four distinct techniques: unit testing, functional testing, business rules testing, and integration testing. Unit testing focused on individual functions and repository methods in isolation. Functional testing verified end-to-end feature workflows across the UI, Riverpod state layer, and Firebase backend. Business rules testing validated the domain-specific constraints that govern medication data, adherence logging, and user data isolation. Integration testing confirmed that all modules — authentication, medication management, daily check-in, local notifications, and theme persistence — work correctly when wired together as a complete system.

All tests were executed on a physical device (OPPO Reno12 5G) running Android 16, which is the target platform for the current implementation milestone. The results documented in this chapter provide confidence that the ForeSeeMe codebase is stable, data-consistent, and ready for extension into the planned 60–100% feature phases.

## **5.1 Unit Testing** {#5.1-unit-testing}

Unit testing verifies the smallest testable components of the software in isolation. For ForeSeeMe, this means individual validation functions, repository methods, provider handlers, and utility helpers. The purpose is to ensure each unit behaves correctly and consistently before it is combined with other modules. Catching defects at this level is far cheaper than discovering the same defect after full integration, and the deterministic nature of unit tests makes them straightforward to repeat whenever the codebase changes.

The following sixteen unit tests cover the Authentication System, Medication Management module, Daily Check-In module, Local Notification Service, Theme Management provider, and the GoRouter navigation guard. Each test specifies the related functional requirement, the testing objective, and a table of test cases with expected and actual results.

**Unit Testing 1: validateEmailField() Function**

**Related Requirement:** FR-1.1 – Email / Password Authentication

**Testing Objective:** To ensure that the email field accepts only correctly formatted e-mail addresses.

| No. | Test Case / Test Script | Attribute and Value | Expected Result | Actual Result |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | :---: |
| 1 | Call validateEmailField() with a standard valid address | "user@gmail.com" | Returns true – field accepted | **Pass** |
| 2 | Call validateEmailField() with a missing @ symbol | "usergmail.com" | Returns false – validation error shown | **Pass** |
| 3 | Call validateEmailField() with an empty string | "" | Returns false – required-field error shown | **Pass** |
| 4 | Call validateEmailField() with trailing whitespace | "user@gmail.com " | Whitespace trimmed; field accepted | **Pass** |

## **5.2 Functional Testing** {#5.2-functional-testing}

Functional testing validates complete user-facing workflows from the UI layer through to the Firebase backend. Where unit testing confirms that individual functions work in isolation, functional testing confirms that the entire feature — form input, Riverpod state, repository call, Firestore write, and UI response — works as a coherent whole. Each test in this section was executed manually on the OPPO Reno5 5G, following the implemented user flows described in Chapters 3 and 4\.

Ten functional test blocks are documented below, covering the authentication flow, Google Sign-In, the full medication management lifecycle, daily check-in behaviour, real-time streaming integrity, local notification delivery, theme persistence, screen navigation, and Firestore data isolation.
